paragraphs.heading: Velocity has a direction
paragraphs.text: Velocity measures how fast something moves and in which direction. That makes it a vector: you need both a size and a direction to pin it down. Speed is only the size part, telling how fast but not which way. Everyday speech often swaps the two words, but physics keeps them apart.

paragraphs.heading: The basic formula
paragraphs.text: Over any stretch of time, an object's average velocity is how far its position changed, Δs, divided by how long that stretch lasted, Δt. Written out, v̄ = Δs/Δt. Position change is counted in metres and time in seconds, so velocity comes out in metres per second.

paragraphs.heading: Never more than average speed
paragraphs.text: Average velocity can never be bigger than average speed. The reason lies in what each one counts. Distance travelled only ever goes up. Displacement, the overall change in position, can grow, shrink or even turn around.

paragraphs.heading: Reading it from a graph
paragraphs.text: On a graph that plots position against time, average velocity has a neat picture. Take the two times that open and close the period, mark those points on the curve, and join them with a straight line called a secant. The slope of that secant is the average velocity. The slope of the tangent line at one point gives the instantaneous velocity instead.

paragraphs.heading: Average versus instantaneous
paragraphs.text: Instantaneous velocity is a separate idea that can seem odd at first. It can be pictured as the velocity an object would keep if it stopped accelerating at that exact moment. Average velocity, by contrast, is worked out over a whole period of time.

paragraphs.heading: When velocity stays constant
paragraphs.text: A velocity is constant only when both speed and direction stay fixed, so the object moves in a straight line at a steady speed. A car going round a circle at a steady 20 kilometres per hour has a constant speed but not a constant velocity, because its direction keeps changing. Any change in speed, direction or both counts as acceleration, so that car is accelerating.
